data.name: panGEMic
data.detailed_description:
It's the mid 1980's, the rich kids have a Commodore 64 and the rest of us have to make do with the rubber keyed under powered Sinclair ZX spectrum.

panGEMic is a game created in the spirit of the day, it's the kind of game you'd expect to see on the speccy.



Collect all the gems while avoiding anything that moves or is pointy, do it in the time limit or face the 'Red Skull'. Collect the coin at the end to finish the stage.

Limited lives means you need to tread carefully while keeping one eye on the timer, extra lives will spawn on some stages so grab them while you can.

Make use of the screen edges to warp from left to right, you'll need to know this to complete some tricky stages and avoid enemies.



  • 9 Steam achievments
  • 25 Challenging stages over 4 Worlds
  • Authentic 16 colour ZX spectrum colour palette
  • Fully rebind-able controls
  • Supports controllers (recommended)
  • 5 suitably retro music tracks
  • Free game
  • For PC & MAC

Best played with a controller

reviews.review:
panGEMic is a small retro platformer that feels like something I could have found on an old ZX Spectrum. The whole game is built around collecting every gem in a stage while avoiding enemies, hazards and anything else that can kill me. I also have a time limit to worry about, so I cannot just slowly walk around looking for the safest route. It is a very simple idea, but the game gets a decent amount of mileage out of it.

What I like most is how quickly the levels get me thinking. I have limited lives, a timer counting down and enemies moving around the screen, so I need to work out a route instead of just reacting to everything as it happens. The screen edges can also warp me from one side to the other, which becomes important in some of the trickier stages. I like mechanics like that because they are simple enough to understand immediately but still give me another thing to consider when I am trying to finish a level.

The presentation is probably the most convincing part of the retro theme. The game uses a 16 colour ZX Spectrum style palette and keeps the graphics very simple, which suits the small stages and quick gameplay. The music follows the same idea with five deliberately retro tracks. I would not call it visually impressive, but I think that misses the point. It is clearly trying to recreate the feeling of an old home computer platformer rather than make a modern game with fancy graphics, and I think it does that well.

There are 25 stages spread across four worlds, which gives me enough levels to properly learn the mechanics and see the difficulty increase. The game is also completely free, and I get nine achievements to work towards if I want to push myself further. I appreciate that there is no unnecessary progression system added just to make the game seem bigger. I am simply completing stages, getting better at the movement and trying to deal with the increasingly awkward enemy patterns. It is a very straightforward structure, but I think that works in its favour.

The main problem for me is that the simplicity can also make the game feel limited. Once I understand the basic rules, there are not many new mechanics being introduced to completely change how I play. The difficulty does increase, but a lot of the challenge comes from tighter timing and more dangerous layouts rather than a huge amount of new content. Losing a life can also be annoying when I make a small mistake, especially when I am already close to collecting everything. I think the game is more enjoyable in short sessions because playing it for too long can make the repetition more noticeable.

I also think the old school design will not appeal to me every time. The controls are intentionally basic, the levels are small and the one hit style of danger means I have to be careful almost constantly. There is something satisfying about finally getting through a stage that has been giving me trouble, but there are also moments where I feel like I am repeating the same attempt simply because I made one bad movement. A controller is recommended, and I can see why because the game feels much more natural when I have precise control over movement.

Overall, panGEMic is a charming little retro platformer that knows exactly what it wants to be. I like the quick levels, gem collecting, time pressure, limited lives and screen wrapping, and the ZX Spectrum inspired presentation gives it plenty of character despite how basic everything looks. It is not a particularly deep game and the limited variety eventually becomes noticeable, but the difficulty gives me a reason to keep trying when I want a quick old school challenge. Considering that it is completely free, I think it offers a fair amount of entertainment without trying to pad itself out with unnecessary features.

Rating: 7.2/10
